title: Aliases: stop typing the same forty characters
summary: Build the handful of aliases that experienced people actually use, including one that shells out, and learn how to read an alias someone else wrote.
mental_model: An alias is a config key under `alias.`. If the value starts with `!`, git hands the whole thing to a shell instead of treating it as a git subcommand — that is the only rule you need to read anyone's dotfiles.

steps.title: The graph command nobody wants to retype
steps.why: This is the canonical history view. It is also 70 characters long, which is why almost nobody types it more than once before aliasing it.

steps.title: Alias it
steps.why: `alias.lg` becomes `git lg`. Aliases live in config like anything else, so `--global` makes it available in every repo on the machine.

steps.title: The short ones that pay for themselves daily
steps.why: `st`, `sw`, `br` and `last` cover most of a working day. Keep them short — an alias you have to think about is worse than the command it replaces.

steps.title: Aliases that take arguments
steps.why: Arguments are appended to the end of the expansion. So `git unstage app.py` becomes `git restore --staged app.py`. No syntax needed — until you want the argument somewhere other than the end.
steps.expect: app.py drops out of the staged column.

steps.title: The bang alias, for anything git cannot express
steps.why: A leading `!` runs the value as a shell command from the repository root. This is how people build aliases that pipe, loop, or call other tools — and how you should read one you find in someone's dotfiles.
steps.expect: Branches listed newest-first, which plain git has no single flag for.

steps.title: Read back what you built
steps.why: `git config --get-regexp alias` prints the whole set. Worth running on any machine you inherit — it explains a lot of otherwise mysterious commands in someone's shell history.

verify.label: a shell alias starting with ! is set
verify.hint: the value must begin with ! for git to hand it to a shell

verify.label: app.py was unstaged using your own alias

pitfalls: You cannot alias over a real git command — `git config alias.status ...` is silently ignored.
A `!` alias runs from the repository root, not your current directory. Relative paths in one will surprise you.
Aliases are per-machine config. They do not travel with the repository, so never write documentation that assumes them.
Quoting an alias with a format string differs between shells. If it breaks, set it by editing ~/.gitconfig directly.
cheatsheet: arguments append to the end automatically
shell out for anything git cannot express
